overview: The atlas labels one 900 to 1000 layer “Sindh,” but its decoded 16-position polygon is not the lower Indus region or today’s Pakistani province. It includes tested Umarkot, Mithi, Nagarparkar, Bhuj, Lakhpat, Gandhidham, the central Rann, Barmer, and Tharad. It excludes Mansura, Aror, Banbhore, Thatta, Karachi, Hyderabad, Sehwan, Larkana, and Sukkur. Read the color as an editorial bucket across the Thar-Kutch corridor, not a surveyed border or uniform state. The historical doorway was more complicated: Habbarid emirs ruled from Mansura; Multan followed a separate political and religious course; ports connected inland producers to the Indian Ocean; and Kutch had its own changing settlement and environmental history. Archaeology recovers streets, houses, a reservoir, workshops, ceramics, and imported wares, while tenth-century geographers describe named cities, crops, clothing, trade, and languages. Their urban and court-facing reports do not speak for every farmer, pastoralist, fisher, craft worker, woman, or child. At 1000 the exact id disappears and most tested polygon points become “rajput-kingdoms.” Habbarid rule did not demonstrably fall that year, so this card treats the endpoint as a map seam and keeps communities in view.

periods.title: 900 to 915: a map begins amid divided power
periods.summary: The atlas first draws its Sindh polygon in 900. Archaeological histories describe Saffarid and then Samanid claims over the wider province, yet neither controlled it effectively. Mansura in the south and Multan in the north operated as nearly independent principalities, already making one solid color misleading.

periods.title: 915 to 930: al-Masudi crosses the region
periods.summary: Al-Masudi’s first recorded journey in 915 to 916 crossed the Indus valley, Punjab, Sind, and India’s western coast. A later study associates his Mansura report with Umar ibn Abdullah, but its large army and village totals remain a traveler’s transmitted claims, not a census.

periods.title: 930 to 943: communities exceed dynastic labels
periods.summary: Evidence for these years is uneven. Religious history reconstructs Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist, and other communities from scattered texts and names rather than population counts. The Habbarid court at Mansura was one institution within a much broader society, while Multan and frontier zones followed different trajectories.

periods.title: 943 to 951: al-Istakhri describes Mansura
periods.summary: Al-Istakhri’s tenth-century geography presents Mansura as roughly a mile square, encircled by a branch of the Mihran. It records date palms, sugar cane, sour citrus, mangoes, Muslim inhabitants, and clothing compared with Iraq, while rulers adopted styles the author considered Indian.

periods.title: 951 to 960: routes connect unlike places
periods.summary: Geographical writing placed Mansura, Debal, Multan, Aror, and other towns within routes rather than one homogeneous culture. Kutch and the Rann also opened toward Gujarat and older Persian Gulf connections. Political, ecological, and commercial regions overlapped without sharing a single everyday life.

periods.title: 960 to 970: religious politics diverge
periods.summary: MacLean’s reconstruction treats Ismaili activity in Multan as a distinct tenth-century development rather than a description of all Sind. Mansura’s Habbarid polity and varied religious communities continued on different terms. The evidence warns against turning one city’s affiliation into a belief map for the atlas polygon.

periods.title: 970 to 976: Ibn Hawqal compares cities and rulers
periods.summary: Ibn Hawqal’s account, written after 976, describes Multan as smaller than Mansura, fortified, fertile, and less carefully cultivated. It presents the two amirs as politically independent while both acknowledged Abbasid spiritual authority. These are comparisons of named principalities, not a single economy under the atlas polygon.

periods.title: 976 to 982: knowledge is compiled across distance
periods.summary: The anonymous Persian Hudud al-Alam was completed in 982 for a prince in Guzgan. It organized the known world from earlier works and a planned map rather than personal travel everywhere. Its existence shows how Sind entered wider learned geographies while reminding readers to separate compilation from eyewitness report.

periods.title: 982 to 985: al-Muqaddasi writes Mansura
periods.summary: Around 985, al-Muqaddasi called Mansura Sind’s capital and provincial metropolis. His Arabic description mentions wood-and-clay buildings, a stone-and-brick congregational mosque on teak pillars, markets, river water, learning, trade, fierce heat, and many mosquitoes. It is a named urban report, not a regional household survey.

periods.title: 985 to 1000: the dynasty outlives the atlas endpoint
periods.summary: Mansura remained under Habbarid rule as the atlas approached 1000. The State Bank chronology carries the dynasty to 1010, while another scholarly reconstruction ends it in 1025. Both place the political ending after this card’s seam, so 1000 cannot honestly be narrated as a fall.

sections.title: Read the polygon before trusting its name

items.text: The exact index has one generated state id, “sindh,” named “Sindh,” with approximate dates 900 to 1000. It is present in one border file and still lacks a researched summary, card, review, or accepted override. The imported summary describes the modern province, so it is unsafe medieval copy.

The 900 target is one Polygon with one ring, 16 decoded positions, and bbox 68.07128071280712, 22.777107514890602 to 73.42813428134284, 27.15540484530348. Its decoded geometry SHA-256 is 4fe97d38b91de7376dfb4be244cd046ac5f297b8a0814e291d9feea462193e1d. Those are reproducible display-data facts from a coarse digital shape, not historical survey coordinates or proof of control.

Tested Umarkot, Mithi, Nagarparkar, Bhuj, Lakhpat, Gandhidham, the central Rann, Barmer, and Tharad lie inside. Mansura, Aror, Banbhore, Thatta, Karachi, Hyderabad, Sehwan, Larkana, Sukkur, Mirpur Khas, and Badin do not. The label therefore misses the Indus core normally central to medieval Sind history.

At 800, the exact id is absent. The future polygon’s tested points are split among the atlas’s “hindu-states” and “vallabhi” layers, while Indus urban probes fall under “abbasid-caliphate.” At 900 those same Indus probes become “saffarids,” yet they remain outside the new Sindh polygon.

At 1000, the target disappears. Most former member probes become “rajput-kingdoms,” while surrounding points divide among other atlas layers. By 1100, Indus centers sit in “soomra-emirate,” but Kutch and Thar probes again divide. Neither seam licenses a claim that one population vanished or changed identity overnight.

sections.title: Rulers, capitals, and power with boundaries attached

items.text: The Habbarid family established independent authority at Mansura around the mid-ninth century. The reviewed archaeological monograph credits Umar with expanding the great mosque and building the government palace and other structures. That court history belongs to lower Sind, especially Mansura, which the atlas polygon itself excludes.

A Pakistan Archaeology synthesis says caliphal authority assigned Sind to the Saffarids in 871 and that Samanids replaced them around 900, but neither exercised effective control. Its conclusion is two almost independent principalities, Mansura and Multan. The atlas instead colors different places and must not overwrite that distinction.

Al-Masudi traveled through the Indus region in 915 to 916. A modern historical study associates his Mansura account with Umar ibn Abdullah but warns that a solitary report cannot settle every political question. Even impressive army, elephant, and village figures should be read as transmitted claims, not audited statistics.

Religion and politics were not synchronized across the region. MacLean’s study treats Ismailism in Multan separately from religious life in Habbarid Mansura and from Hindu and Buddhist communities. A ruler’s sermon, judge, or mosque can reveal an institution without revealing the belief of every household beyond its walls.

A British Museum authority file knows Muhammad, amir of Sind, principally through coins and dates him only broadly between 800 and 1000. That is a useful warning about ruler lists: a name on silver is strong evidence for authority, but a broad catalogue date cannot supply an exact reign or border.

sections.title: Trade, farming, river routes, and the Indian Ocean

items.text: Banbhore occupied an old Indus-channel setting near the coast. The Government of Sindh describes a long-lived early Islamic port site, but the identification with written Debal remains a scholarly proposal rather than a settled fact. Its location still makes it crucial evidence for exchange between river country and sea routes.

Banbhore’s museum inventory includes eighth-century storage jars, glass from the Muslim-period sequence, and Chinese pottery dated broadly from the ninth through twelfth centuries. Those ranges cross this card’s interval but extend beyond it. They prove long-distance material connections more safely than they date any single family’s cupboard.

Ibn Hawqal compares Multan with Mansura: Multan was smaller and fortified, its produce cheap and its territory fertile, though cultivated less carefully. This is useful evidence for urban markets and farming contrasts, but one geographer’s comparison cannot be pasted onto inland farmers, desert pastoralists, port workers, or Kutch settlements.

Al-Istakhri records date palms, sugar cane, a very sour apple-sized fruit, and mango-like fruit around Mansura. Cheap abundance in a geographic text signals productive cultivation and markets, though it gives no farm sizes or labor shares. Please resist inventing a medieval fruit salad recipe from a crop list.

A specialist irrigation history proposes that Habbarid stability supported restored inundation channels, expanded cultivation, and urban surpluses. The author reconstructs rather than directly measures this system, so the cautious conclusion is dependence on shifting Indus water and managed flood flows, not a precise tenth-century canal map or acreage total.

sections.title: Homes, food, clothing, and ordinary work

items.text: A departmental Mansura excavation report identifies a numbered house measuring 370 by 196 feet. Its exceptional scale proves that substantial residential architecture existed, not that every family occupied anything similar. Excavated urban buildings are especially visible; huts, temporary shelters, rural compounds, and mobile pastoral homes survive less generously.

A 1981 Mansura field diary indexes wheat, animal and bird bones, a cooking furnace, storage jar, copper bowl, grinding or rubbing equipment, and household fittings. Because an index is not a finished stratigraphic synthesis, these finds illuminate tasks and foods at the site without guaranteeing that all belong to 900 to 1000.

The 1982 diary adds fish bones, cock bones, eggshell, date-palm material, a grinding stone, fireplaces, jars, and rubbish pits. That is excellent evidence for people cooking, eating, storing, and discarding things. It is poor evidence for a universal menu, and the published index alone cannot assign every item a precise decade.

Al-Istakhri compares ordinary clothing at Mansura to Iraqi dress while saying rulers adopted hair and tunic styles he considered Indian. The contrast suggests connected fashions and deliberate elite display. It does not tell us how women, laborers, children, pastoralists, or people in Kutch dressed across seasons and social ranks.

Habbarid silver was tiny: the State Bank Museum describes fractional dammas of about 0.5 gram and says the mint, Mansura or Multan, is not named. Small coins made daily exchanges possible, but their survival favors durable money over perishable wages, baskets, cloth, and lunch. Archaeology always keeps odd receipts.

sections.title: Families, social life, belief, and unequal voices

items.text: Mansura excavators recorded residential rooms, verandas, courtyards, partitions, and water fittings. These spaces hosted repeated domestic activity, probably by households, but walls cannot disclose whether residents formed nuclear, extended, servant-containing, or workshop households. Architecture supplies a stage for family life, not a complete cast list.

Excavated bangles, beads, rings, jewelry, and decorated objects show bodily adornment and personal possessions. A 1966 diary also records shell and glass bangles and a copper finger ring. Assigning each object automatically to women or to one faith would turn modern expectation into evidence, so the card leaves owners open.

MacLean reconstructs Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist, and other religious lives from uneven textual traces. Conversion unfolded over time, and named scholars or rulers are more visible than villagers. The responsible social picture is plural and changing, with disagreement and coexistence, rather than a sudden replacement of everybody’s practice after conquest.

The congregational mosque, government complex, market areas, streets, workshops, and residential quarters at Mansura structured different kinds of gathering and authority. Archaeology makes institutions visible but rarely records who was excluded, who swept the floors, or who cared for children nearby. Social life must be described with those silences intact.

Government excavations across fourteen seasons recovered coins, artifacts, jewelry, and other objects over ruins extending several kilometers. Their variety suggests rulers, craftspeople, traders, worshippers, and households sharing an urban landscape. The short official summary does not sort those finds by gender, status, religion, or exact century, so neither does this card.

sections.title: Children, education, languages, and a written sample

items.text: The 1966 Mansura diary indexes children’s teeth, a toy rattle, a toy grinding mill, animal figurines, game objects, and small balls. These are rare direct openings onto childhood and learning through imitation or play. Mixed deposits and object labels prevent assigning every toy to a particular child or decade.

No surviving source in this packet provides enrollment lists, lesson schedules, or a typical child’s school day. MacLean can identify scholars, hadith study, judges, and religious networks, but that is adult institutional history. Children likely learned through households, work, worship, and play; exact curricula would be speculation.

Tenth-century geographers report Arabic and Sindhi at Daybul, Mansura, and Multan. That statement supports multilingual urban life, not one standardized Sindhi spelling system or universal fluency. Ports and courts needed language crossing, while many spoken varieties, occupational vocabularies, and rural speech communities remain invisible in the brief reports.

An Indira Gandhi National Open University unit reports that a Hindu ruler commissioned an Arabic scholar from Mansura in 886 to translate the Quran into a local language. The episode matters for translation, but no manuscript is presented here, and “local language” should not be silently converted into a known modern Sindhi text.

Written-language sample, about 985, Mansura: Arabic “المنصورة هي قصبة السند ومصر الإقليم” (al-Manṣūra hiya qaṣabat al-Sind wa-miṣr al-iqlīm), literally “Mansura is the capital of Sind and the metropolis of the province.” This is al-Muqaddasi’s learned geographic prose, not a sample of every resident’s speech; recensions and spellings vary.

sections.title: Medicine, health, diet, and honest absences

items.text: This packet found no securely dated 900 to 1000 Mansura hospital, physician’s kit, prescription, or medical school. That absence in reviewed evidence does not mean nobody treated illness. It means the card should not import Baghdad’s famous medicine into Sind without a local source, however tempting the golden-age shortcut may be.

Urban access to water mattered for health even though medieval builders did not know germ theory. Archaeology describes wells, covered drains, channels, baths, and a lake-side source at Banbhore and Mansura. Such systems sustained neighborhoods but also required upkeep. They identify infrastructure, not water-quality tests or equal access.

Mansura’s 1966 excavation index includes a bathing tub, water outlet, terracotta drainpipe, soak pipe, and soak pit. These features show people managing water and dirty runoff. Their precise dates and household relationships require fuller stratigraphic publication, so they are evidence of site practice rather than a citywide sanitation guarantee.

Wheat, fish bones, bird bones, eggshell, animal remains, and date-palm material can help reconstruct diet, seasonality, and environment. The 1982 diary lists them but does not provide a complete quantified food study. Bones also preserve better than porridge, so the surviving menu is biased toward the crunchy evidence.

Al-Muqaddasi calls Mansura’s air mild and winter easy, yet also emphasizes severe heat and many mosquitoes. That memorable complaint is period evidence for discomfort, not a diagnosis of malaria or another disease. Apparently even a tenth-century geographer knew that mosquitoes can review a city without being invited.

sections.title: Water, waste, baths, and the toilet question

items.text: Treccani’s archaeological synthesis describes Mansura blocks with independent water supply through wells and drainage through underground channels. Residences had wells, often with terracotta collars, plus covered lined drains. This is substantial urban engineering evidence, but coverage varied by block and cannot be extended to villages or the Thar-Kutch polygon.

A 1977 to 1978 field diary records water supply, a terracotta pipe, drains, rubbish, pits, and ash among residential remains. These features show maintenance and disposal work, the unglamorous engineering that lets a city function. The diary index does not prove a unified municipal sewer or identify who cleaned it.

Banbhore’s fortified town bordered a lake or reservoir used as a major water source, while access routes connected the city to it. Such storage helped a port survive dry periods and crowded activity. It also demanded protection from silt and waste, although the archaeological plan cannot tell us a daily cleaning schedule.

Near Banbhore’s mosque, channels may have served ritual washing and latrines; the interpretation is explicitly uncertain. Archaeologists also report baths elsewhere at the site. So the safest toilet answer is “possibly here, with plumbing,” not a claim that every home owned a private bathroom or that the drain smelled delightful.

Mansura’s 1982 diary separately indexes a terracotta soak pit, rubbish pits, a covered drain, and street surfaces. Together with other seasons, this shows multiple strategies for water and waste. Because features come from excavated portions and mixed occupation phases, citywide access and tenth-century dating remain open questions.

Four bronze door knockers found near Mansura’s government complex bear Arabic religious text and a Habbarid ruler’s name. Archaeological comparison argues for local manufacture and a thriving metalworking bazaar. Their fierce faces and petal-shaped rings made an official doorway announce itself before anyone even knocked.

A British Museum Mansura coin weighs only 0.50 gram and measures 11 millimeters. Its Arabic inscriptions occupy several lines, with a crescent and dot among the designs. Minting legible authority onto such a tiny silver surface was a technical achievement, although catalogue dating remains broadly 800 to 1000.

Banbhore excavators recovered more than 4,000 carved ivory, animal-bone, and shell fragments linked to jewelry and furniture manufacture. Other materials were locally made or imported from Iran. The concentration reveals skilled work and Indian Ocean connections, while the project cautions that the site’s identification with written Debal remains debated.

Glass fragments at Banbhore are being studied compositionally to distinguish raw materials, technologies, and possible links with Middle Eastern and eastern production. That scientific caution matters: a pretty shard is not automatically an import. Archaeometry can test whether craftspeople remelted, copied, traded, or locally produced materials.

A recent Banbhore synthesis records ivory and bone-working waste, glass, metallurgy, mother-of-pearl objects, vessels, and Chinese porcelain in later sequences. These finds show production, distribution, and redistribution, not merely consumption. Their broad stratigraphy crosses centuries, so individual pieces should not all be stamped “tenth century” for convenience.

sections.title: Conflict, environmental change, and the 1000 seam

items.text: Al-Masudi’s report portrays Mansura’s ruler fighting Med groups and maintaining soldiers, cavalry, and elephants. A historical thesis reproduces the figures but notes how thin the evidence is. Warfare affected frontier communities, animals, food supply, and labor, not only rulers; exact force totals remain claims rather than verified rolls.

Banbhore’s heavy walls, bastions, and gates materialize defense, while Mansura diaries record arrowheads, spearheads, daggers, and sling balls. Weapons prove preparation and episodes of danger more readily than a particular battle. Fortification also redirected everyday movement, taxation, work, and refuge for people living inside and beyond the walls.

The Indus delta and Rann changed physically. Historical geography describes silting that transformed an open bay near Badin toward salt marsh by the eleventh century. Such change altered channels, pasture, cultivation, and access to ports. It did not respect the straight chronological boundary of an atlas snapshot.

Sources disagree on the Habbarid ending. The State Bank museum gives 1010; the reviewed archaeological monograph gives Mahmud of Ghazna’s conquest in 1025. Neither supports a fall in 1000. The difference should stay visible because compressing it into a confident date would hide the limits of the evidence.

The 1000 map removes “sindh” and assigns most former member probes to “rajput-kingdoms”; by 1100, the atlas separately colors a Soomra emirate on the Indus plain. These are editorial layers across a century gap. Farmers, traders, craft workers, families, languages, and water systems continued through the software seam.

ending.text: At 1000 the exact “sindh” feature disappears. Most tested Thar-Kutch member points become “rajput-kingdoms,” while the historically central Indus probes, outside the target all along, change from “saffarids” to other atlas layers. The map encodes no conquest or population break at this boundary. The override therefore leaves fell null and names no single successor. Ports, farms, workshops, households, languages, religious communities, and water systems continued through the editorial seam.
